transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Ryland Barton.
Polls are still open across much of the country for this year's midterm elections, but they
began to close in Indiana and Kentucky this hour.
Relatively few voters have positive things to say about President Trump's economic leadership,
according to an AP voter poll.
About two-thirds of U.S. midterm voters say Trump's policies have worsened economic conditions
in the U.S., while only about three in ten say they've improved things.
NPR's congressional correspondent Claudia Grisalis joins me now.
Hi, Claudia.
Hey there.
So both midterm history and President Trump's low approval ratings find Democrats in a good
position tonight.
What are the other factors that you're watching for?
Well, we're watching voter mood very closely.
There's a lot of focus on what many see as a bad economy, and this cuts across all electorates.
Some are blaming the party in power, and President Trump for these economic woes, such as high
gasoline prices and grocery prices.
Also, Trump asked voters to imagine he was on the ballot, so we'll see how much sway
he still has with those Republicans.
What would Democrats focus on should they retake one or more of the chambers of Congress
tonight?
Right.
Many have said a divided government will allow them to bring Trump's second-term agenda to
a grinding halt that is challenge what they see as a corrupt administration, concerns
of self-dealing for himself, his family and associates through investigations and other
efforts.
They also want to address his expansion of executive powers, the dismantling of key portions
of federal government, and they want to install affordability measures, but that's going
to be a tall order.
All right.
NPR's Claudia Grisalis.
Thank you so much.
Thank you.
Voters across metro Atlanta are making their selection for senator and governor amongst
other highly contested races.
Marlon Hyde from member station WABE reports on why voters say they're showing up to the
polls.
A light rain cleared up over the Buckhead Public Library in the northern part of Atlanta,
just as 78-year-old Reza Zahidi finished voting.
Originally from Iran, Zahidi says he's conservative and voted for candidates that support the
war in the Middle East.
100 percent of America is taking the rights that these oil prices are temporary.
Meanwhile, on the south side of Atlanta, health care was huge for 49-year-old Maui Bigelow.
We know that there are millions of Georgians that cannot afford health care.
There are millions of Georgians like me who do not have health care.
Affordability is another concern of Georgia voters as well.
For NPR News, I'm Marlon Hyde in Atlanta.
More on that AP voter poll.
About two-thirds of voters said Trump's tariff policies have hurt the national economy.
Views of President Trump's priorities more broadly and his capabilities as a leader are
also mostly negative.
More than half of voters say President Trump's not a strong leader, does not fight for people
like them, does not have the right priorities, and does not have the mental capability to
serve effectively as president.
A rebound for some influential tech stocks helped keep the U.S. stock market steady today,
despite a fall for Apple and mixed trading elsewhere.
This is NPR News.
Federal authorities charged an Oklahoma man with sending hundreds of letters containing
non-hazardous white powder to public officials.
The FBI says in a court filing that so far, the powders have turned out to be yeast or
flour, though not all letters have been fully tested.
The man is charged with conveying a hoax and mailing threatening communications.
A gallon of gasoline costs over $4, diesel's not far from its record high in September,
which was above $6.50.
As companies report their profits, this court of the nation's biggest oil refiner told investors
it raked in sky-high revenue.
NPR's Willa Rubin reports.
Marathon Petroleum Corporation made more than $7 billion this quarter.
That's about seven times what it made this time last year.
Most of its money came from refining, turning crude oil into stuff we use, gasoline, diesel,
jet fuel, other plastics.
Marathon's operating costs were flat compared to this time last year.
But, the war in Iran and Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries have reduced how much
gas and diesel has gotten to global markets, raising prices.
The marathon's earnings call executive said gas and diesel inventories are still relatively
low, and they expect the high margins on refining to continue well into next year.
Marathon said it's raising its quarterly dividend to investors 10 percent.
Willa Rubin and PR News.
Collins dictionary has named "mogging" as its word of the year.
The slang term means to outshine someone or something, and is often used playfully by
young people.

topics.text: Polls close in Indiana and Kentucky as midterm voting continues nationwide
AP voter poll finds most midterm voters say Trump's economic policies have worsened conditions
NPR's Claudia Grisalis outlines Democrats' midterm position and agenda if they win Congress
Atlanta voters cast ballots in Senate and governor races, citing health care and affordability
AP poll finds most voters say Trump lacks strong leadership and right priorities
Stock market holds steady as tech rebound offsets Apple's decline
Oklahoma man charged with mailing hundreds of letters containing non-hazardous white powder
Marathon Petroleum profits surge to $7 billion, citing Iran war and Ukrainian refinery strikes
Collins Dictionary names 'mogging' its 2026 word of the year
